title: The Russia Stability Tracker
gist: CNAS's September 2026 Russia Stability Tracker finds Putin's grip on power still firm but domestic stability less certain, as economic stagnation (growth of at most 1% in 2026, high inflation and rates), war fatigue and Ukrainian long-range strikes on refineries causing fuel shortages converge. Five of ten pillars are weakening — elite cohesion, information control, economic well-being, security-service capacity and Putin's popularity — while repression and the absence of an alternative keep the regime intact; experts warn the danger is multiple challenges arriving at once.

themes.theme: Convergence of challenges to the regime

insights.claim: Putin's regime retains a firm grip on power, but Russia's domestic stability is now less certain because economic stagnation, public concern about the war and Ukrainian long-range strikes are converging — and research shows convergent challenges, not single shocks, destabilize long-standing autocracies.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Russian regime-risk is rising from a low base; tail scenarios matter for energy markets and Ukraine war outcomes.
insights.quote: Political science research suggests that long-standing authoritarian regimes are less likely to be destabilized by a single challenge alone
insights.locator: While the group’s experts agreed

insights.claim: Of ten tracked pillars of Putin's stability, elite cohesion, information control, economic well-being, loyal security services and Putin's popularity are weakening, while absence of an alternative, exit of the discontented, an apolitical military, repression and the 'besieged fortress' narrative are unchanged.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: A structured checklist for monitoring Russian political risk over time.
insights.locator: Pillars of Putin’s Stability

insights.claim: UCLA's Daniel Treisman lists parallel risks — spending outrunning revenue with international borrowing closed, rising corporate debt especially in military industry and regional budgets, inflation stalling Central Bank easing, strike-driven fuel shortages and a weaker ruble, and clan infighting — none regime-threatening alone but dangerous if they arrive at once.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Watch Russian fiscal deficit, corporate/regional debt and the ruble as stress indicators.
insights.quote: None of these problems is individually regime-threatening. The danger is that multiple challenges arrive at once and prompt spiraling mistakes.
insights.locator: There is no visible political threat

insights.claim: CSIS's Maria Snegovaya judges the situation sustainable because Russia is regaining battlefield adaptation advantages and the war in Iran has kept oil prices high.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: High oil prices from the Iran war are a key prop for Russia's finances — a fall in oil would raise Russian instability.
insights.quote: the war in Iran has kept oil prices high
insights.locator: Russia is moving in a negative direction

themes.theme: Economic stagnation and Ukrainian refinery strikes

insights.claim: Russia's wartime boom has turned to stagnation, with 2026 growth expected at no more than 1 percent and persistently high inflation and interest rates straining businesses and households.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Weak Russian macro backdrop limits fiscal room for the war and raises social strain.
insights.locator: Economic conditions have deteriorated

insights.claim: Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries have caused gasoline shortages, hours-long petrol-station queues and higher transport and logistics costs, which the Kremlin cannot hide from the public.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Refinery outages reduce Russian product output — relevant for diesel/gasoline balances and crude export volumes.
insights.quote: Explosions from Ukrainian strikes on Russian soil and especially the long lines at petrol stations cannot be hidden from the public.
insights.locator: At the same time, Ukraine’s increasing strikes

insights.claim: Russians withdrew billions of dollars from banks this summer amid fears the Kremlin could restrict or seize deposits to finance the war, and restaurant traffic has declined significantly, including in Moscow.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Deposit flight is an early warning sign for Russian banking-sector stress.
insights.locator: Russians are increasingly pessimistic

insights.claim: VTsIOM polling in July found 66 percent of Russians think the most difficult times are still ahead, up from 60 percent in May, with only 13 percent believing the worst has passed.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Rising pessimism signals weakening consumer confidence and war support.
insights.locator: Russians are increasingly pessimistic

insights.claim: Arrests of senior figures around Putin allies Arkady and Boris Rotenberg, apparently fueled by war and shrinking resources, signal that even elites close to Putin are not immune as they compete over a smaller pie.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Rising expropriation risk inside Russia's elite — property rights increasingly contingent.
insights.locator: It remains the case that most

insights.claim: A new decree lets the Russian state take temporary control of companies deemed to have failed to protect critical infrastructure from security threats, which influential players could use as a pretext to seize smaller firms.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Heightened nationalization/asset-seizure risk for any residual corporate exposure to Russia.
insights.locator: Likewise, the government’s new decree

insights.claim: Internet tightening — mobile shutdowns and Telegram and VPN restrictions — has hurt Russian businesses and disrupted officials' work, reflecting friction as security services prioritize regime security over economic costs.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Security-first policy is imposing growing economic drag on Russia's digital economy.
insights.locator: There is also evidence of friction

themes.theme: Security services strain and military control

insights.claim: Russia's Interior Ministry reported a staffing shortfall of more than 200,000 personnel in 2025, worsened by better-paying defense-industry jobs, which could hamper responses to localized unrest and let small incidents escalate.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Policing capacity is a weak link if unrest emerges, raising escalation risk.
insights.locator: There are no significant indications

insights.claim: Returning war veterans could raise crime and add demands on an overstretched police, while the Kremlin manages veterans' political integration via its 'Time of Heroes' program.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Post-war demobilization is a medium-term social-stability risk for Russia.
insights.locator: The Russian military remains largely apolitical

insights.claim: The military remains apolitical as the Kremlin rotates senior commanders rapidly — military district commanders now serve only about a year on average — preventing independent power bases.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Low coup risk from the military supports regime continuity.
insights.locator: The Russian military remains largely apolitical

insights.claim: Rumors that FSB head Aleksander Bortnikov may retire and of a change at the top of the Interior Ministry could stoke friction among competing FSB departments.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Leadership changes in security organs are a signal worth monitoring for elite instability.
insights.locator: Rumors also abound about a possible change

insights.claim: VTsIOM recorded the sharpest weekly drop in Putin's approval since the full-scale invasion in late June, from 70.4 to 66.9 percent and to 66 percent by early July, while Levada showed a fall from 79 to 74 percent — versus 80-plus percent in the previous tracker.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Declining approval is a measurable leading indicator of regime stress.
insights.locator: In the last stability tracker

insights.claim: Putin's remaining support appears passive rather than enthusiastic, and most Russians favor negotiations to end the war — though Levada finds they want it ended on Russia's terms.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Domestic pressure for a deal is building but not on terms Ukraine would accept — limits near-term peace odds.
insights.locator: Even as his stated approval ratings

insights.claim: King's College's Sam Greene argues Putin has a credibility problem: Russians no longer see an avenue to end the war — they can't win on the battlefield and hopes Trump would bail them out have faded — and overreaching beyond unknown credibility limits could trigger a crisis.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Credibility erosion makes a policy misstep (e.g., new mobilization) a potential crisis trigger.
insights.quote: Putin doesn’t just have a policy problem; he has a credibility problem.
insights.locator: The Duma elections were designed

insights.claim: The Kremlin benefits from a 'besieged fortress' narrative in which Europe has replaced the US as main antagonist, with Russians now naming Germany as most hostile; Ukrainian strikes initially produce rallying effects but may feed war fatigue over time.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Russia-Europe hostility is entrenched — supports sustained European defense spending.
insights.locator: The Kremlin continues to benefit

themes.theme: Repression and no alternative to Putin

insights.claim: The regime banned Yabloko, the only anti-war party, from the Duma elections — reversing course after polling showed it would likely enter parliament — and United Russia's large margins signal opposition is futile.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Political channels for dissent are closed, reducing odds of an orderly policy change.
insights.locator: The absence of an alternative to Putin

insights.claim: Repression targets even narrative challengers: VEB.RF chief economist Andrei Klepach was fired after warning Russia could not win a prolonged economic war of attrition, and Yabloko's Lev Shlosberg and Maxim Kruglov got 11- and seven-year sentences.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Suppressed internal economic warnings mean official data/narratives understate stress.
insights.locator: Repression remains a critical pillar

insights.claim: Syracuse's Brian Taylor and others judge an insider coup far-fetched and mass protests even more so, concluding repression works and Putin stays in power barring a real crisis or black-swan event.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Base case is regime continuity and continued war — don't price Russian regime change.
insights.quote: Yet an insider coup is far-fetched, and mass protests even more so. Repression—and the fear of it—works.
insights.locator: Russia is becoming less stable

insights.claim: Georgetown's Angela Stent cites an estimated over 1 million Russians killed or severely wounded in the war — a catastrophic toll that strains society even with compensation to families.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Manpower losses constrain Russia's labor market and long-run growth.
insights.locator: Despite all of the military, economic

insights.claim: Columbia's Timothy Frye argues the Kremlin's other legitimation tools — government performance, propaganda and the ruler's personal popularity — are increasingly blunt, leaving costly repression as the main instrument.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Rising reliance on repression implies higher fiscal and elite costs for regime maintenance.
insights.locator: Challenges to the Kremlin are rising
